notes.meaning: Saul fully agreed with the killing of Stephen and was glad to see him die. That very day a violent wave of persecution attacked the believers in Jerusalem, forcing almost all of them to flee into the countryside of Judea and Samaria while the apostles stayed behind. God used this painful scattering to carry the good news of Christ far beyond the city walls.

Devout men carefully gathered Stephen's body to give him a proper burial, weeping and mourning deeply for him. These men showed great faith and courage by honoring the fallen martyr in the middle of fierce danger.
Saul began tearing the church apart like a wild beast hunting its prey. He marched from house to house searching for believers, violently dragging off both men and women to throw them into prison.

The believers who were driven from their homes did not go into hiding or give up. Everywhere they traveled, they openly shared the good news of Jesus with the people they met. Hardship only helped spread God's message farther.

Philip, one of the seven helpers chosen in Jerusalem, went north to a city in Samaria. Jewish people usually avoided Samaritans, but Philip boldly announced to them that Jesus was the promised Savior.

Crowds of Samaritans listened closely and with one mind to what Philip was teaching. They paid close attention because they heard his message and watched the amazing miracles God performed through him.

Evil spirits screamed loudly as they were forced out of many troubled people. Philip also healed many men and women who were paralyzed or could not walk. These wonders proved that God's power was breaking the grip of darkness and restoring broken bodies.
The entire city was filled with great happiness. The people rejoiced because their sick loved ones were healed, but even more because their hearts had received the saving truth about Jesus.
Before Philip arrived, a man named Simon had lived in the city practicing sorcery and dazzling the people. He bragged about himself and claimed to possess extraordinary spiritual power.

People from every walk of life, from the poorest beggar to the most important ruler, listened eagerly to Simon. They fell for his deception and declared that he was a direct display of God's great power.

The crowds remained devoted to Simon because his magical tricks had held them spellbound for a very long time. His occult arts had clouded their minds until the true light of the gospel broke through.

When the Samaritans heard Philip preach about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they believed his words instead of Simon's lies. Both men and women were baptized to show they had turned to the Lord.

Even Simon professed faith in the message and was baptized alongside the others. He stayed close to Philip, utterly amazed by the real miracles and signs that easily proved greater than his old magic tricks.

differ.view: Simon had a real but short-lived faith, somewhere between true faith and pretending, like seed that is choked before it ripens; it lacked denial of self.
His baptism brought no new birth, but if he later truly repented, its grace could become real without being baptized again.
Simon was never truly saved; real faith shows itself by repenting and keeping on, and outward Christian behavior does not prove conversion.

notes.meaning: The apostles who were still in Jerusalem received word that the Samaritans had welcomed God's message. They sent Peter and John to visit them and officially welcome them into the wider church family.

As soon as Peter and John arrived, they prayed for the new Samaritan believers to receive the Holy Spirit. They asked God to bless these converts with the same spiritual gifts that believers in Jerusalem had experienced.
The Holy Spirit had not yet fallen on any of the Samaritans in an outward, visible way. They had simply been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus as genuine believers.

differ.view: The Assemblies of God teaches that the baptism in the Holy Spirit is a distinct gift that comes after a person is saved and baptized in water. This second experience empowers believers for ministry and witness, often beginning with the sign of speaking in tongues (praying in a spiritual language given by God).

Reformed teachers explain that God held back this visible gift for a unique, historical moment to unite Samaritan believers with Jewish believers under the apostles' care. For ordinary Christian life today, every believer receives the Holy Spirit the moment they put their faith in Jesus, rather than waiting for a separate second stage.

notes.meaning: Peter and John laid their hands on the believers, and they received the Holy Spirit. This showed everyone that Samaritan believers were fully accepted by God as equal partners with Jewish believers.

differ.view: Believers receive the Holy Spirit in a distinct experience after conversion that brings supernatural power for Christian service.
God temporarily delayed the coming of the Spirit until the apostles arrived so the Samaritan believers and the Jewish believers would remain one united church rather than splitting.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Catholic rite of confirmation looks to this passage, where the Spirit is given through prayer and the laying on of hands.

notes.meaning: Simon watched carefully and saw that the Holy Spirit was given when the apostles laid their hands on people. Wanting this influence for himself, he pulled out his money and offered it to Peter and John.
Simon asked the apostles to sell him the power to impart the Holy Spirit to anyone he touched. He treated the Holy Spirit like a magical secret that could be purchased to make himself famous.
Peter rejected Simon with strong indignation, telling him that his silver could perish right along with him. God's gifts are given freely by grace and can never be bought with money.
Peter bluntly told Simon that he had no share or part in this ministry. His heart was crooked and insincere before God, showing that he was motivated by pride rather than true faith.
Peter commanded Simon to turn away from his wicked greed and beg the Lord for mercy. He held out hope that God might still pardon the evil thought in Simon's heart if he genuinely repented.
Peter warned Simon that his life was full of bitter poison and locked tight in the chains of sin. His selfishness and desire for control proved that he had not truly surrendered his soul to God.

Frightened by Peter's severe words, Simon begged the apostles to pray for him so that God's judgment would not fall on him. He was terrified of being punished, yet he showed little sorrow for his actual sin.

After Peter and John had shared their testimony and preached the word of the Lord, they began their journey back toward Jerusalem. Along the way, they stopped to share the gospel in many Samaritan villages.

An angel sent from the Lord told Philip to leave Samaria and travel south to the desert road that leads from Jerusalem down to Gaza. Philip obeyed right away without even knowing why God was sending him to such an empty place.

Philip headed down the road and met an important court official from Ethiopia who managed all the wealth of Candace, the queen of the Ethiopians. This man had traveled all the way to Jerusalem to worship the true God at the temple.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars note that the official held high royal status under the queen mother in Meroe, and his story highlights the early church welcoming individuals previously excluded from full religious fellowship.

notes.meaning: While riding home in his chariot, the Ethiopian was reading aloud from the scroll of the prophet Isaiah. Even during a long journey, he made good use of his time by seeking God in the Scriptures.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some read him as a literal eunuch and see the story showing that people with all kinds of bodies were welcome in the early church. The servant's humiliation and lack of descendants in Isaiah may have matched his own situation.

notes.meaning: The Holy Spirit told Philip to walk right up to the chariot and stay close beside it. Philip listened carefully and followed the Spirit's prompt guidance.
Philip ran alongside the carriage and heard the official reading the words of Isaiah the prophet. Philip called out and asked him directly if he understood what he was reading.
The official humbly replied that he could never understand the passage unless someone guided him. He warmly invited Philip to climb up and sit with him in the chariot so they could talk.

The passage of Scripture he was reading described a suffering servant led like a sheep to the slaughterhouse. Just as a quiet lamb stands still before its shearers, this servant did not open his mouth to protest.

The reading continued by saying that justice was denied to him in his humiliation and his earthly life was cut short. The prophet asked who could ever describe his future family when he was taken away from the earth.
The official asked Philip to explain who the prophet was describing in these verses. He wanted to know whether Isaiah was speaking about his own pain or pointing forward to someone else.

Starting right from that passage in Isaiah, Philip told the official the good news about Jesus. He explained that Jesus was the suffering servant whose death and resurrection brought salvation to the world.
As they traveled together down the road, they came across a body of water. The official eagerly pointed to it and asked what would prevent him from being baptized right then.

Philip told the man he could be baptized if he believed with all his heart, and the man replied that he believed Jesus Christ is the Son of God. Sincere faith in Jesus is the essential requirement for baptism.

differ.view: Some argue the verse should be kept, because it records a genuine early confession of faith.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching notes that this verse reflects an ancient confession shaped by the early church's baptismal liturgy, demonstrating that adult baptism requires a personal confession of faith.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Textual scholars point out that this verse is absent from the oldest Greek manuscripts and was probably added by early copyists to record an explicit baptismal confession.

notes.meaning: The official ordered the chariot driver to pull over and stop. Both Philip and the official stepped down into the water, and Philip baptized him as a new follower of Christ.

differ.view: Going down into the water points to baptism by immersion, where the person being baptized is placed fully under the water.
Going down into the water simply means stepping down from the carriage to the water's edge and does not prove immersion.

notes.meaning: When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord miraculously carried Philip away, and the official never saw him again. The Ethiopian continued his journey home overflowing with deep joy because he had found the Lord.

differ.view: Some think this was not a miracle of movement, but the Spirit strongly urging Philip to leave quickly for other work.

notes.meaning: Philip suddenly found himself at the coastal town of Azotus, which was ancient Ashdod. From there he traveled north, preaching the gospel in every town along the coast until he arrived at Caesarea.
